articles.title: Curry, Wembanyama o Edwards, entre los 'reyes' del NBA 2K27: Estos son los líderes en cada estadística del juego
articles.standfirst: 2K publicaba el top 10 de jugadores en diferentes aparatados
articles.summary: 2K publicaba el top 10 de jugadores en diferentes aparatados
articles.body: La NBA acabó la temporada anterior, la 25/26 por todo lo alto con el anillo de los New York Knicks. Pero esta temporada que viene, la 26/27, no ha empezado de diferente manera, ya que hemos tenido un inicio espectacular, primero con el draft en el que tres nuevos españoles han llegado a la mejor liga de baloncesto del planeta, Aday Mara, Sergio de Larrea y Baba Miller, y más tarde con una agencia libre que nos ha dejado movimientos históricos que prometen cambiar la competición por completo. Giannis Antetokounmpo aterrizando en los Miami Heat era el primer gran movimiento que veíamos en la NBA de cara a la temporada que viene, el que pensábamos que, de lejos, sería el más impactante, pero no. Ya que el bombazo de Jalen Brown y LeBron James fichando por Philadelphia 76ers han dado un vuelco radical a una conferencia este más fuerte de lo que estábamos acostumbrados a ver. Este inicio de temporada marcado por el draft y la agencia libre marca, como decíamos, el inicio de una nueva temporada en la NBA, pero el lanzamiento del NBA 2K también, ya que el mejor juego de la mejor liga de baloncesto del planeta sigue el ciclo de la competición. Y es que ya tenemos las primeras noticias sobre el NBA 2K27, como la portada de Victor Wembanyama, las primeras imágenes oficiales del videojuego, o, por supuesto, las primeras estadísticas de los jugadores. Como por ejemplo las medias de algunos jugadores, en concreto las de los rookies, los que llegan a la NBA este año con especial expectación y en la que no vemos a Aday Mara entre los 10 mejores de este año, algo que nos podíamos esperar ya que fue elegido en la posición números 12. Independientemente de esto, estos son los 10 mejores novatos de la NBA según las valoraciones de 2K27. Pero además de las medias también, como es tradición cada año, 2K publica el top 10 de jugadores en estadísticas concretas, sin importar la valoración general, solo ese apartado en concreto del jugador. Por eso, en los apartados defensivos siempre tenemos a algunos habituales que aparecen año tras año, auténticos especialistas en la defensa que copan estas listas. El primero de ellos, como no podía ser de otra manera si hablamos de tapones es Victor Wembanyama, el que con un 99 en este apartado cuenta con los mejores números en tapones, algo lógico pues es insuperable. Pero en la 'otra defensa', la del perímetro y los robos, también tenemos un claro vencedor, Ausar Thompson, el alero de los Pistons que es un muro, tanto en la realidad como en el videojuego. Pero en estas listas de defensores también tenemos a otros 'sospechosos habituales' como Kawhi Leonard, Derrick White, Dyson Daniels, Alex Caruso o Rudy Gobert, jugadores que siempre han estado entre los mejores defensores de la competición, también en el NBA 2K. Como no podía ser de otra manera, si hay mejores defensores también hay mejores atacantes, por lo menos si tenemos en cuenta solamente el tiro, y estos, por lo que vemos cada día en las pistas de la NBA son indiscutibles. Decimos esto porque como el mejor tirador de media distancia tenemos a Shai Gilgeous-Alexander con 99, algo lógico, ya que en la realidad parece que el canadiense no puede fallar desde esa zona. Y si esta estadística tenía un dominador claro la del triple más todavía, ya que si hay un especialista desde la línea de 3 puntos en la NBA, en toda la historia de la liga, ese es Stephen Curry, el base de los Warriors que con 99 de valoración en este apartado deja muy lejos al segundo de esta lista, Kon Knueppel, el que cuenta con un 94. Hablando de ataque, al igual que tenemos a los mejores tiradores, también tenemos a los mejores manejadores, esos jugadores que hacen lo que quieren cuando tienen el balón en las manos. Y al igual que Curry lleva siendo años el 'rey del triple', Kyrie Irving es el del manejo de balón, también este año en NBA 2K27 con una valoración en este apartado de 99. Pero si mezclamos esta gran habilidad y la potencia, la velocidad, es decir, el apartado de velocidad con el balón en las manos, también tenemos a un habitual en esta estadística, uno de esos jugadores que en cuanto tienen el balón en las manos son inalcanzables si 'arrancan la moto'. Hablamos de De'Aaron Fox, el que tiene un 97 en este apartado en NBA 2K27. Y para terminar vamos con el apartado más espectacular, tanto en la realidad como en el videojuego y este es el de los mates y el salto vertical, esta habilidad que hace que nos levantemos del asiento si de verdad un jugador lo domina. Como por ejemplo Amen Thompson, el alero de los Rockets que lidera la lista de salto vertical en el NBA 2K27 con un 99 en este apartado junto a Tobi Lawal, el de Dallas, que cuenta con los mismos números. Pero más espectacular es cuando el salto vertical acaba en canasta, en un mate espectacular, un apartado de juego que llama siempre mucho la atención y que es una de las cualidades de Anthony Edwards, el que lidera la lista de 'dunkers' de NBA 2K27 con un 97.

articles.title: Ni Hugo González ni Aday Mara, los españoles de la NBA se quedan fuera de 'las élites' del 2K27
articles.standfirst: Nuestros representantes en la mejor liga del mundo no están entre los mejores en el videojuego
articles.summary: Nuestros representantes en la mejor liga del mundo no están entre los mejores en el videojuego
articles.body: Como ocurre en cada inicio de la temporada de la NBA, el 2K, el mejor videojuego sobre la liga, también arranca una 'nueva vida' con el lanzamiento de una nueva edición. Y con este comienzo también tenemos mucha nueva información como por ejemplo los mejores jugadores del videojuego en cuanto a la valoración o los mejores jugadores en diferentes aspectos del juego como el tiro de tres, la defensa de perímetro o el manejo de balón, por ejemplo. Pues bien, de cara al NBA 2K27 tenemos malas noticias para nuestro país, por lo menos si hablamos de este videojuego, ya que ninguno de los españoles aparecen entre los mejores jugadores por valoración general, tanto en la lista global como la de los rookies, pero tampoco en los apartados de robos, tapones, defensa del perímetro, tiro de media distancia, tiro de tres, manejo de balón, velocidad con balón, salto vertical o mates, todas las categorías sobre las que tenemos rankings para 2K27. Y es que esta noticia pese a que sea negativa no nos pilla por sorpresa ya que ninguno tiene todavía esa consideración de estrella dentro de la liga. Pesa a esto podíamos pensar que por ejemplo Santi Aldama, un jugador bien considerado dentro de la NBA, podía estar entre los 100 mejores jugadores por media de la liga, y más viendo que los primeros en entrar en este top contaban solamente con un 81 de media. Pero además de este, si nos vamos a listas más específicas podíamos haber tenido representación como por ejemplo en la de los rookies, ya que Aday Mara, uno de los jugadores con más hype de este draft, elegido en el número 12, no se ha conseguido colar en el top 10 de novatos en 2K27. Y es que aunque quizá es soñar demasiado, el recién elegido por los Thunder podría haber tenido un hueco en el top 10 de taponadores por esa envergadura y capacidad para taponar tiros, aunque seguro que, aunque no esté ahora, lo veremos en un futuro. Para terminar nos vamos con Hugo González, el que ya en su primer año impresionó a toda la NBA por su capacidad de trabajo y defensa, por eso podíamos soñar con su presencia entre los 10 mejores de la liga en cuanto a robos, o mejor todavía, en defensa en el perímetro, la gran cualidad que ha mostrado el de los Celtics en su breve paso por la NBA, aunque, al igual que decíamos con Aday, si no está todavía en esta lista, estamos seguros de que lo veremos en el futuro.

articles.title: Strange New Worlds' Film Noir Episode Looks Cool, Sure, But Also Reminds Us That a Gimmick Is Not Enough to Carry an Hour of TV
articles.summary: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Episode 4 Recap and Review: “A Case of Chiaroscuro” is a high-concept, low-impact installment of Strange New Worlds that looks cool, sure, but also reminds us that a gimmick is not enough to carry an episode.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 4, “A Case of Chiaroscuro.”

Alright, here’s the thing about Strange New Worlds. For whatever reason, at some point showrunners Akiva Goldsman and Henry Alonso Myers decided that gimmick episodes were what this show needed. After a brilliant first season of adventure-of-the-week episodes, Season 2 featured occasional segments like “Those Old Scientists,” a crossover with the animated series Lower Decks , and “Subspace Rhapsody,” a musical episode, which lit a fire under the notion of what a modern episode of Star Trek could be. And that was great.

But somewhere along the way, the gimmicks became the focus, and frankly, they’ve grown kind of tiresome. I was really hoping with Season 4 that we’d just get back to regular weekly adventures. So when this week’s episode, “A Case of Chiaroscuro,” began and everything was in black and white, my mind immediately went to Yellow Alert. By the time we were on Mat'aar XII, the planet of the week (which is a kind of throwback to a film noir and/or Casablanca world), my inner Red Alert was in full effect. IT’S ANOTHER GIMMICK EPISODE.

When a newly promoted Commander Una Chin-Riley (Rebecca Romijn) leads an away team of Dr. M'Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) and Ensign Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding) to retrieve a probe that’s strayed into Klingon space, the group find themselves stuck on Mat'aar XII, where not only does everything appear to be black and white to our heroes (due to the infrared something something radiation of the system), but also you have to dress up like knock-off Humphrey Bogarts and Carmen Sandiegos in order to fit in.

Look, it’s a cute enough idea I suppose. The Original Series did go to a gangster planet after all. And the visuals of the episode are pretty cool. But as “A Case of Chiaroscuro” labors through its beats to hit the tropes of the genre(s) it’s working to imitate, the hour just winds up feeling like a Cinema Studies 101 midterm paper: High-contrast and shadowy black and white photography? Check. Doppelgänger characters? Check. A central bar/cafe where conspirators and their foes can congregate? Check. Corrupt local authorities? Check. And so on and so on. The thing is, like that middling paper from the kid who only half paid attention in class, the episode really gets its film noir chocolate mixed up in its wartime/romance film peanut butter.

But whatever, let’s not quibble about that. The real problem here is that Una’s struggle isn’t really fleshed out enough. I understand that she’s torn between wanting to help the local resistance fighters who are pushing against the Klingon occupation they are enduring, and I also understand that this is a particularly personal issue for her due to her own childhood when it was the Federation who were seen as the occupiers by some of her fellow Illyrians. And yet, there’s little here that makes me feel much for Una’s current (or past) situation.

Indeed, it’s Olusanmokun’s M'Benga who once again steals the show, even though he’s depicted here as more of an advisor to both Una and Uhura rather than given his own plotline. The idea of the kindly physician who is also a skilled warrior and an adept spy is so darned cool as the good doctor counsels the young Uhura in how to navigate this strange (new) world while also reminding Una that she can’t let her responsibility to the resistance movement overtake her oath to Starfleet. He even gets the best line of the hour: “My calling is medicine, healing people. It's the great mystery of my life that some of my strongest skills lie in opposition to that calling.”

The B story involves Christina Chong’s La’an, who’s been flirting with going over to the dark side all season, obsessing over what she thinks might be clues that there’s a traitor onboard the Enterprise. The thing is, nobody else buys her theories, not even her friend-with-benefits-but-actually-her-boyfriend Spock (Ethan Peck). Again, it’s a fairly low-impact plotline that culminates in the revelation that, whew, La’an is not crazy, but also, whoa, she just lied to Captain Pike (Anson Mount) to cover up the truth. Pike seems to maybe know there’s more going on here, and trusts La’an to do the right thing, but still…

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

So if Una’s next step up the promotion ladder is captain, how long until she gets her own ship and leaves the Enterprise for good? (Never to be mentioned or seen again, by the way.)

In her opening log, Una says that they’re at risk of “re-starting a very Cold War,” but shouldn’t that be “re-starting a shooting war”? The Klingons and the Federation are in a state of Cold War by the time Kirk is in command of the Enterprise, and presumably that’s been the situation since the end of the war depicted in Star Trek: Discovery …

The chief Klingon here is Kor, who I guess is supposed to be the Kor from The Original Series and Deep Space Nine who was played by the late, great John Colicos. Fine, I guess? (The House of Kor was also depicted in Star Trek: Discovery, although Kor himself was not.)

Speaking of Discovery, the shuttle Una and the gang take in this episode is the Cervantes, which according to Memory Alpha is a Stamets-type vessel. It’s gotta be named after either the Discovery’s Paul Stamets (who is considered lost and MIA at this point in the timeline) or possibly the real-life mycologist Paul Stamets who the character is named after. Right?

articles.title: The Corvette Grand Sport X delivers Porsche 911 performance for a fraction of the price
articles.summary: The Corvette Grand Sport X can help heal our automotive differences with its power and performance.
articles.body: My drive of the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport X began under oily black clouds, a torrential weather front releasing its grip on Manhattan — an inauspicious start for any mega-powered sports car. Rain pelted the waterlogged pavement, as I set course for the mountain-man roads of the Catskills, then on to Long Island and New England over three days. Fortunately, this Grand Sport, a name synonymous with value among Corvette fans, was the first of its kind: A 721-horsepower super-hybrid with a brainy, confidence-boosting AWD system. I popped the Corvette into Sport mode, Wet mode be damned. Finding tire grip galore on the Palisades Parkway, I realized the “X” badge on those wide flanks had changed the forecast to “fun.”  As a track-centric mid-engine sports car, the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport X is hardly representative of mass-market transportation. But the GSX still has something hopeful to say — or shout, with every seismic blast of its new LS6 V-8 engine — about the world’s renewed love affair with hybrids.  People have always made a statement about who they are, or the person they want to be, through the car they drive or the one they dream of owning. Beetle or BMW, Porsche or pickup, Stingray or Subaru. These choices are more fraught than ever as a zero-sum game emerges between EVs and internal combustion engine cars.  You can watch that standoff unfold on YouTube, with drag races between Teslas and seemingly every ICE car since the Model T. When I came of age in Detroit, true sports-car fans scoffed at such reductive straight-line contests, the equivalent of an arm-wrestling match to determine the most gifted athlete.  On a broader level, it doesn’t have to be this way. Electrified cars like the Grand Sport X can help change the conversation and build common ground on today’s scorched earth. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_Rear-7-8.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_Rear-Driving.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_Side-Profile-Driving.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS-Launch-Edition_Rear-Wide.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS-Launch-Edition_Spoiler.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Corvette’s sophisticated algorithms bring two often-warring tribes together. There’s electric business in the front, and a gasoline party in the back, with no physical connection between the electrified front axle and petroleum-powered rear wheels. Finely coordinated teamwork and integration makes the GSX the latest all-wheel-drive hybrid sports car that feels like an unfair fight against purely gasoline models.  GM could use some teamwork on the hybrid front. The company currently has just two gas-electric models. Both are Corvettes. Both use electricity strictly to boost performance, like a hybrid F1 racer, with fuel economy not part of the brief. In America, only hybrids have gained powertrain market share in 2026, with both EVs and pure ICE losing ground. With a record 15.4 percent of the market through June, hybrids are outselling EVs by nearly three to one. Even in China, hybrid sales are growing faster than those of EVs. Three companies, Toyota, Hyundai and Honda, now control 90 percent of this booming US hybrid market. Toyota and Lexus alone sold 600,000 hybrids through June. The windfall has seen Hyundai and Kia post their best overall sales in history, including a 115-percent jump for Kia’s growing hybrid lineup. Caught flatfooted after having gone all-in on EVs, GM is racing to bring fuel-saving plug-in hybrids back to its showrooms, supposedly beginning next year.  The GSX itself replaces the Corvette E-Ray, Chevrolet’s first hybrid sports car. But it’s an entirely different animal. The 650-horsepower E-Ray was a versatile grand tourer: fast and fluid, but a bit of a mellow yacht rocker. The GSX was expressly designed as a track assassin, with heightened power, roadholding, braking, and agility.  What GM engineers call the “baby ZR1X” adopts its electrified front axle directly from the 1,250-horsepower, 233-mph record setter that I tested at Sonoma Raceway. Most every internal part number is identical. But in keeping with the Grand Sport’s reputation as a sweet spot in the Corvette lineup, the GSX coupe’s $112,195 base price is less than half that of a ZR1X at $227,395. For 2027, a non-hybrid, 535-horsepower Grand Sport asks $88,495. That rear-wheel-drive Grand Sport will be more than enough for many buyers.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_Interior-Display-Wide.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS-Launch-Edition_Head-Rest.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_-Next-Generation-V8-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_Badge-Vertical.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GS_Interior-Wide.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Some want more. So the GSX’s  721 horsepower represents a 186-hp bump over a Grand Sport or 2027 Stingray. Add a monumental 655 pound-feet of torque, and the GSX easily tops the 690 horses and 531 pound-feet of a McLaren Artura, a hybrid that starts from around $260,000. As in the ZR1X, the internal bearings in the electric motor were beefed up to handle a higher output of 186 horsepower and 145 pound-feet of torque. Push the GSX’s start button, and the engine crackles to life, before settling into a menacing basso idle. Floor the accelerator, and the  cabin fills with enough pummeling, martial sound to backdrop a Christopher Nolan epic. The electric motor plays its own whirring part, including a metallic overlay of selected frequencies amplified through the audio system. EV backers may believe silence is golden (sometimes it is) and scoff over ICE fans’ unwillingness to give up their thrashing cylinders. What they forget is that an engine’s sound offers not just drama and engagement, but critical somatic cues as to how fast you’re going, and a car’s gear or limits at a given moment. Yes, an EV can digitally imitate those cues. But for now, as with certain music, analog still beats digital among the performance cognoscenti. An optional performance exhaust for $1,995 is a worthy upgrade. Corvette engineers lavished attention on the center-mounted exhaust and its four trumpeting outlets to coax out its most-pleasing harmonic frequencies. Another $2,995 for a front-end lift system is another practical spend, to avoid scraping the low-slung front splitter on every steep driveway.  Displacing 409 cubic inches, the stroked V-8 coincidentally harkens to a bygone age of muscle, when Brian Wilson ticked off the Chevrolet Impala SS’s technical virtues in the Beach Boys’ hit “409.” (Hey, it was the ’60s).  Here in 2026, the LS6 makes that old 409 seem primeval, in tech, power, or efficiency. Pricey forged cylinders can deactivate to save fuel. A lofty 13:1 compression ratio is the stuff of race cars and also contributes to cleaner fuel burn. The engine reduces emissions by 28 percent versus its less-powerful predecessor.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GSX_Front-3-4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GSX_Badge.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27_Chevrolet_Corvette_GSX_Interior-Plaque.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/MY27-Chevrolet_Corvette_Stingray.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The engine’s 520 pound-feet of torque sets a high for any naturally aspirated V-8 in production-car history. This overachiever also becomes the standard power plant in a 2027 Stingray, making this “basic” Corvette even more of a sports-car bargain at $73,495. The engine manages a 25-mpg highway rating, impressive for a Stingray that can nip 200 mph.  As noted, neither the GSX nor the ZR1X gives a hoot about fuel economy. Their adrenalized performance encourages its pilots to feel the same. The GSX topped out at 22 mpg during my drives. It settled in around 15 mpg, and dipped as low as 11 or 12 mpg during barnstorming runs through the Catskills. Whichever automaker can bring a two-seat, truly mass-produced electric sports car to market — whether Porsche or someone else — energy savings will be an easy win for Team Electric. The Corvette’s electric machine is fed by a tiny 1.9-kilowatt-hour battery mounted in the chassis’ spine, between driver and passenger. Again, that battery isn’t about efficiency or solo electric propulsion. Instead, its cells are designed to absorb regenerative energy like a fast-acting sponge, and spit it back out in rapid bursts. The motor fills any gaps in the engine’s output with an unbroken wave of torque, including during paddled upshifts from the eight-speed, dual-clutch automated gearbox.  Chevy cites a launch-controlled run to 60 mph in a sparkling 2.4 seconds, and a quarter-mile in 10.4 seconds at 131 mph. I manage 2.6 seconds to 60 mph, even on lumpy backroads in upstate New York. Those official measures are 0.1-seconds quicker than an E-Ray on both counts, and 0.2 seconds quicker than another track-centric Corvette: the mighty Z06 and its Ferrari-esque, flat-crankshaft V-8. As you’d expect, launch starts are less dramatic than in rear-drive Corvettes, all four tires hooking up with a yawn before you’re hammered into body-hugging bucket seats.  Familiar hardware, including a limited-slip rear differential with selectable Performance Traction Management settings, is retuned for this application. A superlative MagneRide suspension reads the road 1,000 times per second to adjust the viscosity of its magnetic-fluid dampers, and stiffen or soften shocks at individual wheels. The ride is firm but not spine-crunching, especially in Touring mode. Algorithms help dial in electric power for any situation, striving for handling balance and linear power delivery. In familiar tuning disagreements between passionate engineers, every GSX tiebreaker went to the track.  As compared to the E-Ray, “we’re keeping the edgier scenarios where the car feels more ready to pounce, versus a more-docile character,” says Keith Badgley, lead development engineer. [Image: The author’s gray tester. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/1000004069.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Stated simply, electrified front wheels take a major burden off of rear tires, here shod with Michelin Pilot Sport all-season tires in a fat 345/25/ZR21 size. Powerful carbon-ceramic brakes are standard, helping to explain a somewhat eye-opening $23,700 price jump from a standard Grand Sport. Like its ZR1X daddy, the GSX lets me brake deep into corners and jump back on throttle earlier, with fewer worries about the back end getting loose. In the rolling twisties of the Catskills, the GSX felt thrillingly athletic and on-its-toes. Hard-working front wheels palpably yank the ’Vette out of fast corners. Common sense is the only thing that will stop you.  The GSX also adopts the ZR1X’s specialized performance strategies. Hitting a “Charge +” button summons an Endurance mode, ensuring electrified wheels can deliver a consistent AWD jolt over a full tank of fuel, even during track sessions. A Qualifying mode preps the car for the fastest possible lap. Push-to-pass mode offers the full monty of gasoline and electric power on demand. To keep peace with neighbors, a Stealth mode lets the Corvette roll on electric power alone at speeds up to 50 mph.  The energy strategies make it virtually impossible to run the battery below 40 or 50 percent on public roads, no matter how hard you try. Selecting Charge + will also refill the battery over five miles or less of driving, using the gasoline engine and kinetic energy to generate electricity via the motor. Did I mention this Grand Sport makes a great first impression? Rolling into fabled Woodstock, the GSX underscored how the eighth-generation Corvette is (finally) widening its appeal beyond a traditional Boomer, rock n roll audience. I can still quibble with aspects of the C8 design, especially that bluff back end. But the Grand Sports’ 3.6-inch-wider chassis, cavernous side air inlets, and forged aluminum wheels add to its exotic supercar vibe. Everywhere I rolled up in the glowering gray GSX, someone would stop in their tracks to offer questions or compliments. And not just car fans, but people who didn’t always realize this was a Corvette, but were visibly impressed when they found out. Serious fans will recognize a Grand Sport’s traditional hash marks on rear fenders, rendered in classic Admiral Blue on my test car. The Corvette’s reworked interior will also win friends. A new auxiliary screen sits just left of the steering wheel, for easier access to launch control and PTM settings. There’s an intuitive Google-based infotainment system, graphical performance readouts, and the ingenious camera-based Performance Data Recorder to record and analyze track laps using telemetry software. A removable hardtop remains a signature coupe feature, and a GSX convertible starts from $119,195. My GSX coupe started from $122,845 at its richest 3LT trim level. A schmear of options lifted that to $140,080. By old measures, that’s a lot of money for a Corvette. But a Porsche 911 Carrera 4 GTS hybrid, with 189 fewer horsepower, starts from $191,650, and soars past $220,000 with a modest sprinkling of options. And again, the GSX costs roughly half the price of a ZR1X.  From the chip-on-shoulder Corvette to Porsche, Ferrari, Lamborghini and McLaren, buyers who might be ambivalent about EVs are warming to this new breed of hybrid sports cars. Their advantages are becoming harder to resist. For any type of car or SUV, I’ll argue that the hybrid love affair, rather than being seen as a rejection of EVs, is exactly the opposite. It’s a sign that Americans are already willing to meet electrification halfway. The next step becomes that much easier.

articles.title: A Court of Thorns and Roses Is Getting an Original Strategy Board Game, and Preorders Are Live
articles.summary: Take romantasy to the tabletop and fight for favor across the Courts of Prythian.
articles.body:
October is going to be a busy month for A Court of Thorns and Roses fans. The highly anticipated sixth book in the series from Sarah J. Maas is coming out on the 27th, but we're also getting two board games based on the beloved romantasy novel in the weeks before.

A Court of Thorns and Roses - Fate & Favor , from the minds at Goliath Games, is a new strategy board game where 1-7 players fight for power in the fae realm of Prythian. It’s up for preorder at Target for $24.99, with a release date set for October 11th. An ACOTAR Edition of Monopoly , listed for $39.99, is also coming out on October 1.

ACOTAR - Fate & Favor Board Game Now Up for Preorder

A Court of Thorns and Roses - Fate & Favor Board Game

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen a romantasy series get the board game treatment. In fact, Rebecca Yarros' Empyrean series has inspired Fourth Wing versions of Monopoly and Priorities . Instead of being a themed version of an existing game, however, this specific ACOTAR board game is entirely its own thing.

A Court of Thorns and Roses - Fate & Favor is full of familiar places and faces from the book. You play as one of the High Lords or Ladies of the seven Courts of Prythian: Night, Day, Dawn, Summer, Autumn, Winter, and Spring. You will forge alliances from this position, but loyalties can change as you ultimately compete for the most influence over the courts. It’s all about forging your own story and shaping your destiny through character abilities, court powers, event cards, and shifting fate tokens.

Created by genuine fans of the ACOTAR series, incredible detail has been poured into both the gameplay and artwork of Fate & Favor. It looks like tons of fun for fans of the books, but should also be enjoyable for those who haven’t had a chance to delve into this magical world. However, like the books, Fate & Favor is best-suited for ages 14+.

A special “Bookseller Variant” with exclusive packaging will be available at select bookstores in addition to the standard editions that's already up for preorder online. The contents of both editions will be the same.

Monopoly: A Court of Thorns and Roses Special Edition Board Game

Monopoly: A Court of Thorns and Roses Edition Board Game for Adults

As mentioned, ACOTAR is also getting a Monopoly Edition. Several, in fact. There's an Amazon-exclusive green variant , along with the classic red that matches the cover of the first book.

In both versions, the board highlights places from the series rather than your typical locations like Park Place and Boardwalk. It also features golden tokens with items from the book, including Feyre's Bow. Plus, the game offers manors and palaces over houses and hotels.

Preorders for the sixth and seventh A Court of Thorns and Roses books are also available. While neither book has a title yet, book six is out October 27, and book seven drops shortly after on January 12, 2027. Not much is known about the plot, either, but Maas claims the story is “big – really, really, really big."

Danielle is a Tech freelance writer based in Los Angeles who spends her free time creating videos and geeking out over music history.

articles.title: You can now just point at a mess and this robot vacuum will suck it up
articles.summary: A free update brings on-device gesture control and a Gemini-powered voice assistant to the WALL-E-style robot vacuum
articles.body: Matic, my current favorite robot vacuum, just got a big upgrade. The company has launched Matic Cues, which brings voice and gesture control to the robot. Now, you can talk directly to your vacuum to tell it what you want it to do, or just point at a mess to have it spot-clean.  The feature launches today, August 13 at 2 pm ET, and will show as an option in the Matic app under Settings > Matic Cues. The update arrives just ahead of a planned price hike on September 9, which will see the WALL-E-style robot’s price go from $1,245 to $1,495. I’ve been playing with Matic Cues for a day or so, and so far it’s working well. Gesture control is the standout feature here, as it’s something no other robot vacuum offers — the company’s founders are both computer vision engineers who worked at Google Nest cameras, and have been developing the feature since 2017.  [Video: Testing Matic Cues gesture control] It works by waking up the robot with the wake word “Hey, Matic,” then waiting for it to “see” me (by turning toward my voice). I then point to the mess, say “clean here,” and off it goes. I did notice that if I wanted it to target a smaller area, I needed to crouch down to point at it. If I gestured from standing height, it cleaned a wider area, taking longer. It can also follow me, so saying “Hey Matic, follow me,” walking to and pointing at the mess, started a clean-up.  Because it uses the robot’s existing vision hardware — which includes five cameras — gesture control works entirely on-device and is coming to all existing Matic robots. While most robot vacuums let you spot-clean by drawing a zone in the app, I’ve found that method to be imprecise and not useful for quick cleanups. Some can also respond to a “clean here” voice command, but that’s based on the general area where you’re standing; Matic’s gesture-based implementation feels more focused.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_4180-copy.png?quality=90&strip=all] The new built-in voice assistant also worked smoothly in initial testing. Voice control isn’t new on robot vacuums — nearly all work with Alexa and Google and some with Apple’s Siri, and many now have their own onboard voice assistants — including Roborock, Ecovacs, and Narwal. I’ve had mixed success with these long-term. Most require remembering exact commands; while “vacuum the kitchen” is easy to remember, other phrases are less intuitive and less flexible than Matic’s offering.  Matic uses the Gemini API to understand natural language, including commands like “vacuum the inside of the carpet” (thus avoiding the tassels), “clean just the hard floors,” and “clean the toekicks in the kitchen” — something I always want done right after cooking dinner. [Image: The voice assistant can understand natural language; instead of telling it “Return to dock,” you can just tell it to ”Go away.“ https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_8733.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The robot could hear me from a room away and responded promptly — although it took a beat to go off and execute the command. It also doesn’t talk back; instead, its small display indicates it heard you and tells you what it’s doing. I was impressed how many commands it understood, including chained commands, like “clean the kitchen, vacuum the living room, and then mop the bathroom.” It also slunk back to its dock when I said, “Hey Matic, go away.” Handy if it’s underfoot when I’m cooking.  [Image: The voice assistant doesn’t talk back; it displays its confirmation of your command on its screen. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_8731.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] One of Matic’s biggest selling points is that it doesn’t require the cloud and can be used without an internet connection. However, voice control does need both of those. While the company says the “Hey Matic” wake word is processed on-device, meaning no ambient chatter is sent to the cloud, any command after is sent to the Gemini API. A short chime tells you when anything is leaving the device. Mehul Nariyawala, cofounder and president of Matic, says the commands it sends are anonymized, adding that Matic chose cloud processing to support more than 75 languages and a wider variety of commands. The company plans to take the top 20 or 30 most-used commands and bring those locally in the future. Matic Cues is opt in, and you can turn it and the microphones off in settings. The trade-off between more convenience and more privacy is a constant tussle in the smart home. Roborock’s “Hey Rocky” voice assistant is entirely on device, but I rarely use it because it’s just not intuitive. So far I’ve found myself using “Hey Matic” much more frequently, as it’s just easier to talk to. The gesture control also solves a pain point I’ve long struggled with — getting a robot to clean the exact spot I want. For Matic users, this is a worthwhile update, and for those considering pulling the trigger, it’s a new convenience that makes a very good robot vacuum even better. Photos and video by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Diplomacy: The Golden Blade Is a Slimmed-Down, Card-Based Take on a Classic Strategy Board Game
articles.summary: Diplomacy: The Golden Blade is a card game that slims down and shortens the gameplay of the original Diplomacy board game, but it's not necessarily the better for it.
articles.body:
There are few more storied titles in the annals of board gaming than Allan B. Calhamer’s Diplomacy. Reputedly the favorite game of John F. Kennedy and Henry Kissinger, it sees players taking control of one of the great powers of Europe on a map of the continent and fighting it out for military supremacy. Its genius is a 1:1 combat system where pieces simply eliminate other pieces, making it impossible to gain an edge over rivals without an alliance. And it’s in these negotiations and inevitable betrayals that the thrill of the game lies.

The trouble with Diplomacy is that it runs long: with the optimal full complement of seven players, it can easily take up most of a day. Diplomacy: The Golden Blade makes the unlikely claim of retaining all the stab-in-the-dark charm of the original while cutting out the board and slashing the play time to around 15 minutes per player.

Without a board or unit pieces, there’s not a lot to talk about in terms of the box contents. Most of the components are cards, in two different sizes. The smaller ones are unit cards, representing your military forces. The larger ones are order cards that you’ll be playing to enact your decisions against opponents and these have both a picture and a text description of the order. There’s nothing special about the cards, artwork or icons, everything is clear and functional.

More curious of all are a series of punch-out cardboard tags that you use to delineate three rows and seven columns for your play area into which you place your unit cards. They show you what “level” you’ve reached in each row as you fill it with cards. These are fiddly, easily moved during play and, strictly speaking, unnecessary, although they do help all the players read the game state at a glance rather than card-counting.

Each player has a grid outlined by cardboard markers into which they play units cards from their hand. There’s a row for each of the three unit types: army, political and navy. One or two cards gives you level 1 in that unit type, three to six cards gives you level 2 and seven wins you the game. Most turns you’ll only get to play one card into your grid, although the randomly drawn selection in your hand may mean you can’t always play what you want.

However, this being diplomacy, these cards are tangential to the meat of the play, which is order cards. Every player gets an identical set of 12 of these, from which they’ll secretly select two each turn, one for each neighboring player. There are four kinds, one matching each type of unit which you can only choose if you have an equal or higher level in that unit type than that neighbor, and a fourth, “promises”, that you can play anywhere and which generally rely on your neighbor selecting a particular card.

In a turn, you’ll start by drawing a unit card, then there’s a timed five-minute negotiation period where you can make deals with other players – none of which are binding, of course. After that you play your order cards face-down before everyone reveals them all and you go around the table, working out the impact of each pairing. Finally, everyone plays a new unit card to their grid. It’s a simple core loop, easily taught, but the complexity is in the text on the order cards themselves.

Each kind has the potential to achieve different aims. Army orders let you interfere with your target’s units, allowing you to swap cards from your hand with theirs, or even removing played units from their grid. Political cards can give you a leg-up by letting you play an extra unit card or blocking enemy orders that interfere with the cards in your hand. Your naval choices include drawing extra cards, or blocking the most powerful army and political orders. This, then, is a cunningly varied game of rock, paper, scissors in which you get the chance to persuade your foes of your intentions, honorable or otherwise, before selecting an option.

However, it’s the promise cards that really give the game its flavor. Two of them, coalition and accord, give both players vital benefits if they both select a matching card. The former lets you block the order of your other neighbor, while the latter gives you two extra unit cards to draw. Alliance, on the other hand, allows that neighbor to resolve their chosen order against your other neighbor, and it can never be blocked. Critically the card says “may” ... so it leaves you very vulnerable to a sudden stab in the back.

Because you can’t play orders on an opponent unless you match or exceed their level in the matching unit type, players are caught between wanting to try and race towards the seven units needed to win and diversifying to protect themselves. Sometimes that decision is made for you by a lack of unit cards of the desired type, others by what your neighbors are choosing to collect. Either way, picking what to play each turn can be made part of both your ongoing strategy and your ongoing negotiations, bluffing about what you’re holding and might choose to play.

This network of options is, frankly, brilliant. Although it’s initially overwhelming, when you understand the effects of each card you’ll see how they interlock to create a framework of delineated decisions that feel like the free form of maneuvering and fighting in a map. Just like full-fat Diplomacy you can make and break alliances, broker deals, lie, cheat, and backstab to your heart’s content. And because your unit cards are visible to everyone, also just like classic Diplomacy, you’ll certainly have to betray one or both of your neighbors in order to win, because once you reach five or six units cards in a row, everyone will band together to stop you.

So it’s kind of a shame that, while you can still do all the things that drive the original game in this slimmed-down version, it turns out that the real draw of that game is in the cream that’s been lost.

It turns out that racing to seven cards simply isn’t enough time to establish the interpersonal relationships with the other players to really make it feel worthwhile. And it doesn’t matter if your opponents are friends or strangers: you still need time to build up a sense of trust, or develop a really festering feud, within the context of a single game. Without that, the inevitable twists of the knife just aren’t as painful, or as satisfying. Often, in games, the epic feel that players long for can only be delivered by devoting epic amounts of play time to deliver it.

Also, because the game is so short, and there’s a tendency for some players to race ahead in their favored unit type, it’s often a good idea to start getting those stabs in early. Accord is powerful if you pull it off because a bigger selection of cards means it’s more likely you’ll have what you need to push towards your goal. And everyone knows it, so you tend to get a round or two of that before such niceties give way to brutal warfare. Things pick up again towards the end of the game where alliance cards, suggested in the spirit of stopping the leader from getting over the line, can be exploited to give the betrayer a quick leg-up, but backstabbing is so commonplace at this point that it’s rarely the surprise it should be.

articles.title: Satechi’s New Six-Port USB-C Desktop Charger Offers 240W of Power
articles.body:
Satechi has released the ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger , a compact desktop charging brick with six USB-C ports that outputs enough power to keep your favorite power-hungry handheld gaming PC , gaming laptop , smartphone , and more topped up all at once. It even has a screen for those who want to see just how much their gear is drawing.

That 240W is a measure of the device’s total output, not any one USB-C outlet, but Satechi’s new charger can still push out 140W from either of its first two front-facing ports. That’ll charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed and is more than enough to max out the capacity of any handheld gaming PC you throw at it. The 240W Desktop Charger can also offer up to 100W on its second two ports, and up to 30W on the last two. Altogether, it has more ports and faster charging than most of IGN's current favorite USB-C chargers, both in general and for specific devices like the Steam Deck .

Satechi says its display can show the real-time power draw from each port, and that the charger “auto-detects each device’s requirements and balances output across active ports, keeping everything charged efficiently, quietly, and without overheating.” The product comes with a stand that lets you both rest the Desktop Charger horizontally or vertically, with a slight tilt so it’s easier to see the display. The charger comes in one color, Space Black.

The ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger costs $150 and is available now at Satechi’s website and Amazon .

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: The MSI Claw EX is the most important PC handheld since Steam Deck — I still wouldn’t buy one
articles.summary: We review the MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus, a portable PC with Intel’s first dedicated handheld chip. It’s the most powerful truly portable handheld with the best battery life, but trips over certain games and costs far too much amidst RAMageddon.
articles.body: As The Verge’s resident handheld reviewer, I have nearly every portable gaming PC on a shelf in my house. The MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus is now the first one I reach for. Thanks to a next-gen Intel chip and improved MSI design, the Claw EX is the most powerful handheld that truly feels portable. It’s the handheld with the longest battery life, and the first Windows handheld I can trust to sleep and wake reliably.  Like the Steam Deck, when I press the power button, my game is always right where I left off. Unlike the Steam Deck, it can hibernate for days without losing a significant amount of charge.  Performance and battery? Windows and sleep? I wish I could say “you can have your cake and eat it too.” But you can’t. You probably shouldn’t. You can’t because this is a Ferris Bueller Product Review — this handheld costs a staggering $1,800, and you’ll be lucky to find it even at that price. (MSI’s Anne Lee tells me the US should have limited supply sometime this month.) Even if you could, you probably shouldn’t because Intel and MSI and Microsoft didn’t fully stick the landing. This is indeed a milestone for the handheld gaming space. But like actual milestones on a highway, you should probably drive right past. [Product: MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus | https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fclaw-8-ex-ai-cg3em-8-120hz-fhd-1200p-gaming-handheld-intel-arc-g3-extreme-intel-arc-32gb-1tbssd-console%2FJ3P7TXTKW3, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bhphotovideo.com%2Fc%2Fproduct%2F1972338-REG%2Fmsi_claw_8_ex_ai_cg3em_024us_claw_8_ai_cg3em.html, https://click.linksynergy.com/deeplink?id=nOD/rLJHOac&mid=44583&murl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.newegg.com%2Fp%2FN82E16868969012%3Fitem%3DN82E16868969012] The Claw EX does have comfortable grips, I’ll give it that. Those manta-ray-wings wonderfully spread out its weight, to the point that the 1.73-pound (785g) portable feels far more comfortable than the 1.58-pound (715g) Xbox Ally X when I hold it above me in bed. And while a $1,800 handheld should really have an amazing OLED screen, I definitely prefer the Claw EX’s 8-inch 1920 x 1200 48-120Hz VRR screen to the comparatively cramped 7-inch 1080p one in the Allys. The only real problem is glare — the ultra-glossy screen was not great on my road trip this summer. But the controls are merely average, the fan is loud (though it’s whoosh not whine), and those manta-ray grips can buzz my hands when I turn up the speakers. Sound reverberates inside. [Image: I love the grips. Buttons are fine. The joysticks are drift-resistant magnetic ones, but really need tuning. I undershoot and overshoot too much. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-msi-claw-ex-sean-hollister-1-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: Here’s the underside of those meaty grips. I’d prefer grippier, but the stippling is not bad at all. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-msi-claw-ex-sean-hollister-1-6_a1af8c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] No, the Claw EX’s true strengths are performance and battery — but even there, the handheld sometimes let me down. I’ve always loved the phrase “potato graphics.” It’s such a fun way to describe what games look like when your rig is too weak. They’re rough and pasty — like a potato! — even when running smoothly. Or if you turn up the graphics anyway, you get a “slideshow” because your hardware can’t deliver enough frames. The first reason I reach for the Claw EX, before any other handheld, is because I don’t automatically get potatoes or slideshow when I fire up demanding PC games. Like my colleague Jay Peters showed you on launch day, the Claw EX makes games look so much sharper than they do on a Steam Deck, and it’s not just the Deck that’s getting beat. The Xbox Ally X with its AMD Z2 Extreme chip, and the old MSI Claw 8 with Intel Lunar Lake, aren’t playing demanding games smoothly at the 1080p or 1200p resolution of their screens. The Claw EX often can, and I’m seeing around 40 percent more performance than the Xbox Ally X in my tests at 1080p. In many games, like Forza Horizon 6 and Cyberpunk 2077, that’s the difference between playing at native resolution or settling for less. [Table: 1080p benchmarks] When I add a little upscaling, I can even start enjoying games I haven’t been able to enjoy handheld because of potato graphics. I could swing lightsabers in Star Wars Jedi: Survivor and crack whips in Indiana Jones and the Great Circle at good quality with smooth frame rate while binging K-dramas with my spouse. Until, suddenly, I couldn’t — seemingly because Intel’s drivers aren’t playing nice with some games yet. When my Indy visited the Great Pyramid, the Intel chip would simply not run at the wattage I set, and I found spots where the entire game would repeatedly freeze or even trigger a full system hang. In Jedi: Survivor, the game is weirdly stuttery in some areas, even though I get far more resolution and smoother frame rate on the Claw EX than the Xbox Ally X. Until a recent Intel update, Expedition 33 had what looked like intense graphical corruption around its particle effects in the game, turning them into glitchy spots of light. [Table: 720p benchmarks] And you should take Returnal benchmark numbers with a grain of salt, because many graphical effects are entirely missing on Intel. Undergrowth and volumetric fog are barely there; stone objects no longer explode into showers of rock; transparent energy shields are weirdly opaque. The second reason I reach for the Claw EX is that battery life. Like some of its competitors, it has a big 80 watt-hour pack — but the Intel chip can stretch that battery even further than the competition. Take Cyberpunk 2077, for example. To hit a smooth 70fps average at 720p resolution, the Xbox Ally X and the last-gen Claw require around 30 watts of total power, draining their batteries in roughly 2.5 hours. With the new Claw, you can reach that same performance with 21 watts, giving you a whole extra hour on a charge. [Table: Battery life vs. performance] Or take Balatro, the 2D magic poker game that’s become my best-case battery life test. Just by toggling the Claw EX’s “Endurance” mode and setting the screen to 48Hz instead of 120Hz in the Quick Settings menu, I got the handheld’s total system power draw down to just 6.5 watts, enough to last 12 whole hours on a charge. It’s rare to get epic battery life for 2D indie games and performance for triple-A ones from a single chip. But this strength of the Claw EX is flawed, too. When I drain the battery below 15 percent charge with triple-A games, performance dramatically dips. My chip couldn’t maintain its 25W performance mode and switched to 15W instead. That performance didn’t immediately come back when I plugged the handheld in. [Image: Friends don’t let friends run lightweight games at 120Hz. At 48Hz, you can play this same game five hours longer on a charge. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-msi-claw-ex-sean-hollister-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] And though the Claw EX might be the first Windows handheld that properly sleeps and wakes right out of the box, that doesn’t excuse its other Windows woes. I can’t count the number of times I’ve launched a game and been left staring at a black screen, wondering when it’ll finally appear, only to discover it was already running in the background and didn’t show itself. I don’t appreciate having to hold down the Task Switcher button to fix a game that didn’t properly launch full-screen, or having to quit out to desktop mode to download the latest Intel drivers. The handheld should really automatically alert me when they’re available. [Image: MSI’s “AI Engine” setting does seem slightly smarter. It’ll generally run games at 25W TDP, but I see it ramping up when loading and downloading to make wait times shorter. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-msi-claw-ex-sean-hollister-1-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I nearly did a spit take when Windows told me I couldn’t use my handheld’s control panel because, and I quote, “Most of the features in Quick Settings require administration privileges. To use all the features, please switch to an administrator account.” Thankfully, a reboot fixed that. I instinctively reach for the Claw EX, instead of any other handheld, because I’m borrowing it from Intel instead of paying cash — and because I’m willing to tolerate its idiosyncrasies for fewer potato graphics. At $1,800, I wouldn’t. Photography by Sean Hollister / The Verge

articles.title: CMF’s clip earbuds hit the balance between cheap and good
articles.summary: ﻿The CMF Clip Pro are a very comfortable option for those that hate things in their ears.
articles.body: Clip earbuds are an exercise in compromise. It’s an inherent aspect of their design — and physics. They can be more comfortable for people that don’t like something jammed in their ear, but sound response suffers. Ambient awareness is great because you can easily hear the sound around you, which means to hear your own music the buds need to be turned up and potentially leak sound out to your neighbors. For what they offer, they can also get pricey, with popular pairs from Bose, Sony, and Shokz reaching $200. The CMF Clip Pro, though, are under $100, and while they still have those compromises, they handle them well. [Product: CMF Clip Pro | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H72J4TS2?tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fus.nothing.tech%2Fproducts%2Fcmf-clip-pro%3FColour%3DLight%2BGrey] CMF is Nothing’s budget sub-brand, and because it tends to release earbuds in the $40–$60 range, I was expecting the same when I first heard about the Clip Pro. But instead, the Clip Pro are $99 — the same price as Nothing’s Ear 3A that just came out last month with more features (and also more issues). Only a few days after release and the Clip Pro are already on sale at $79, which puts them at the price I think they should be. [Image: Instead of being placed inside the ear canal, the Clip Pro’s speaker sits just outside it and a band wraps around the ear to keep them secure. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268665_Nothing_CMF_Clip_Pro_earbuds_AKrales_0018.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Comfort is the Clip Pro’s big advantage. The flexible band avoids any pinching around the helix, and I didn’t experience any discomfort with how the speaker orb or battery/control capsule sat in and behind my ear. A clip design is the best option for those that have trouble fitting earbuds in their ear canals. Not having the sealed fit in your ear canals, though, affects the sound consistency, and I wouldn’t suggest doing any critical listening on the Clip Pro — or any clip earbuds, for that matter. Even so, the sound balance didn’t negatively affect my listening of my regular playlists and KCSN radio station app. By default, there’s a bass boost, which is necessary without a sealed fit but doesn’t cause the sound to be overly bassy (which other Nothing earbuds can be). There’s a three-band EQ in the Nothing X app to adjust to taste, although as with other Nothing earbuds and headphones, the EQ can be tricky to use. Increasing a slider doesn’t always boost that frequency band, but instead lowers the other frequencies (increasing the bass, for example, actually brings down the mids and highs). It takes some getting used to and extra finagling. The Clip Pro support fixed spatial audio, which adds more space to the sound (I didn’t find it objectionable, but preferred the sound without it), as well as high-res audio over LDAC. The differences with high-res on an open-ear design are so minute, it’s not worth it, especially with any ambient noise around. While listening to my radio app, the DJ’s voice could get difficult to understand during talk breaks with traffic going by. Boosting the volume can solve the problem, but it can also cause the sound to leak out to be heard by those close to you (benchmates on the bus or subway, for example). Turning on anti-leakage mode in the app cuts higher frequencies, but also adversely affects sound quality. The sound only leaks at high volumes, so it’s best to just turn them down. There are multiple options for adjusting the volume in those situations, including directly from your device, with buttons on the capsules that rest behind each ear, or with a dial on the case (assignable in the app). The dial is also a button that can play and pause, skip forward and back, or call up your phone’s assistant. [Image: The Clip Pro’s case has a dial that can control the volume and be used as a button. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268665_Nothing_CMF_Clip_Pro_earbuds_AKrales_0221.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] There isn’t quite enough resistance to the dial, so at times while the case was in my pocket, volume would go up or down by a click or two. I ended up disabling the dial and either using the buttons on the earbuds, which work well although with a slight delay, or just pulling out my phone instead of the case. And with functionality disabled the dial becomes a great fidget toy. The Clip Pro are pretty good with calls and don’t exhibit the buggy functionality I experienced with the Nothing Ear 3A, where the compression on my voice would drastically adjust based on the ambient sound when I started talking. The noise gate is still very aggressive to filter out any surrounding sound and can clip the very end of a word, but when I was speaking at normal volumes while walking down the street, my wife was able to understand me easily. Soft-spoken people might run into issues, though. When I spoke quietly, I sounded very muffled and it took her lots of concentration to try and figure out what I said. That call quality epitomizes the CMF Clip Pro, and it’s the same with their sound. The earbuds are good at what they do under the constraints of the technology. And their comfort, along with their price, make them great when you don’t want something deep in your ear. Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

articles.title: Lanterns Series Premiere Review: How HBO’s True Detective-Style Superhero Mystery Reinvigorates James Gunn's DCU
articles.summary: With a finely honed Dynamic Duo lighting the way, Lanterns serves as a critical return to form for the DCU in its first episode. Read our spoiler-free review.
articles.body:
This is a spoiler-free review of the first episode of Lanterns Season 1. The series debuts on HBO and HBO Max on Sunday, August 16.

It’s safe to say that a lot is riding on the first season of Lanterns . This is one of the first key pieces of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU that isn’t directly steered by Gunn himself. We’ve seen enough by now to know that Gunn himself has a solid handle on the DC brand. Creature Commandos, Superman, and Peacemaker have all been enjoyable. But can this fledgling cinematic universe thrive when he hands the reins over to other creators? Supergirl certainly calls that into question , casting doubt on Gunn’s lofty claims about strong scripts and clear artistic visions being the driving force of this line. The DCU needs a win right about now, and I’m happy to say that Lanterns is ready and able to deliver in its first episode.

Granted, it’s been tough to know what exactly to make of this series. For a franchise as fundamentally fantastical as this one, the prospect of focusing on an Earth-based murder mystery and downplaying the actual Green Lantern elements wasn’t necessarily appealing to all fans. The initial Lanterns trailer did little to assuage the fears of those concerned by that premise. And then co-creator Damon Lindelof really stepped in it with some of his comments, to the point where no less a DC authority than Grant Morrison felt compelled to clap back . Suffice it to say, DC and Warners didn’t really do themselves any favors with the marketing of Lanterns, but the proof is ultimately in the pudding.

Yes, Lanterns is essentially what the trailers and early previews have made it out to be. It’s as much a True Detective and Slow Horses-style murder mystery as it is a superhero drama (and, in fact, features veterans of both shows among its creative team). It’s not necessarily going to appeal to viewers intent on seeing the cosmic side of the Green Lantern mythos on full display. We rarely even see Kyle Chandler’s Hal Jordan put on the costume. And given how ugly and clunky this live-action rendition of the suit really is, that’s probably a good thing. The series generally looks good, but more in that quietly stylized, more grounded True Detective way than because of any budget-busting special effects. In short, Green Lantern purists who want unadulterated, comic book-accurate, ring-slinging cosmic spectacle are setting themselves up for disappointment with this show.

But for those willing to abandon preconceived notions and take Lanterns for what it is, this strange combination of superhero adventure and terrestrial murder mystery works surprisingly well. A lot of that comes down to the chemistry between Chandler’s Hal and his trainee, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart. Hal has never been portrayed as the nicest or most well-adjusted member of the Justice League in various DC media, but here he’s downright hostile and standoffish to his young charge. As much as the first episode lays the foundation for an urgent investigation in the remote town of Rushville, Nebraska, it makes it clear that the real conflict is between Hal and John. One is a cocky, grizzled veteran suspicious that his space cop handlers are trying to replace him. The other is a former Marine with a deep desire for the ring but limited tolerance for shenanigans. To say the two butt heads in the first episode is putting it mildly indeed.

The series leans a lot on that core dynamic, making it crucial that it finds the right actors for the job. That’s one area where Lanterns succeeds unequivocally. Both actors are pitch-perfect in their portrayals of these iconic (if sometimes barely recognizable) characters. Chandler probably isn’t the first name to pop up on anyone’s list of dream Hal Jordan actors. He wasn’t even DC’s original choice for the part , it seems. And were the series striving for a more traditional, youthful take on the character, Chandler would obviously be a poor fit. But that’s not the goal here. This is a version of Hal who’s been active in the DCU for decades and truly feels the weight of those years. Chandler expertly captures that unique blend of exasperation, paranoia, and deep-seated overconfidence that define the DCU’s Hal Jordan. The last thing he feels like doing is training the guy who’s trying to steal his job, and he makes that clear in every interaction with John.

As for John, Pierre brings a quiet, no-nonsense charisma to the screen that contrasts nicely with Hal’s fiery bravado. John is quiet, composed, and stoic, qualities that could make for a very boring role in the wrong hands. Fortunately, Pierre is able to bring enough subtle nuance to the screen that his character never comes across as dull or underdeveloped. He’s reserved, but underneath it all he burns with desire. We see how badly he wants the ring, even if it means putting up with an endless stream of nonsense from his superior officer.

It’s also nice to see the first episode dig a little bit into the racial undertones of this Training Day-esque dynamic. In one scene, a seething John calls his father for advice and is reminded that white men like Hal Jordan have the privilege of being eccentric and difficult. Not so for a Black man trying to prove his worthiness for the most exclusive law enforcement gig in the entire universe. At least at this early stage, it doesn’t appear that Lanterns is going to be steeped in the racial tensions of modern America to the same degree that Lindelof’s previous DC series was , but it’s still satisfying to have that element acknowledged – especially given how important John Stewart was to the early diversification of DC’s comic book universe decades ago.

On the subject of John Stewart, Sr. (played as a young man by J. Alphonse Nicholson and an older man by Sherman Augustus), the premiere teases a very intriguing dynamic there that’s sure to be explored in future episodes. It’s such a common trope for superhero media to paint their protagonists as orphans yearning for a lost father figure. That’s even baked into Hal’s origin story. But Lanterns is clearly striving for something much different with John’s family background, adding in new layers and details that aren’t necessarily taken from the comics. It’s a useful reminder that while the series isn’t afraid to alter the source material in sometimes profound ways, those alterations are about more than simply making Green Lantern practical in a small-screen format.

Once the Hal/John dynamic is firmly established, the premiere sets about laying the groundwork for the murder mystery that looks to be fueling the conflict in Season 1. To be frank, said mystery isn’t the reason to tune into the series, at least at this early stage. It gets the job done in terms of moving the plot from A to B, but for now the conflict is pretty small in scope. It’s mostly about Hal’s uphill battle to convince everyone around him (John included) that the dead bodies in front of them have extraterrestrial ties.

Here again, the various characters and their interpersonal clashes are what make the series shine. Early in the episode, viewers are introduced to another major character in Kelly Macdonald’s Kerry, the no-nonsense sheriff in charge of keeping the peace in the formerly quiet town of Rushville. As much as Chandler and Pierre’s icy dynamic fuels the series in its first episode, there’s also plenty of fun to be had in the equally standoffish relationship between Hal and Sheriff Kerry. There’s all the bickering over jurisdiction and one-sided flirtation you’d expect. Kerry quickly develops into a very fun, likable character who’s every bit the effective foil to Hal that John is.

Rounding out the notable cast members introduced in Episode 1 are Garret Dillahunt as local cowboy/ranch tycoon William Macon and Poorna Jagannathan as another Rushville native named Zoe. Macon serves his purpose as a charming but quietly unsettling antagonist figure with murky ties to the town’s murder mystery. Zoe, meanwhile, quickly strikes up a close bond with John, allowing the series to explore shades of the character that aren’t possible through Hal alone. Rushville is a small town full of interesting personalities, offering plenty of room for growth in the coming seven episodes.

Again, the murder mystery itself gets the job done in terms of plot catalysts, but it’s the characters who tend to shine more than the plot in Episode 1. It is worth noting, however, that the premiere keeps one big reveal under its hat until the final moments. This twist is sure to be as controversial as anything the show has to offer in its debut chapter. But as far as throwing viewers off-guard and hinting at a larger, more ambitious scope for the series, it delivers just what’s needed. If the prospect of plainclothes Green Lanterns loudly squabbling and rubbing elbows with cowboys isn’t enough to lure you in, this twist might just do the trick.
